acuity.responding_to: Stuart Smith: "I think my colleague the Hon Simeon Brown neglected to mention that Lake Onslow is very expensive—there’s no doubt about that." (and the $15.7 billion / cost-overrun argument that follows it)

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chlöe Swarbrick argued that this Government is returning the country to the 1980s-90s 'trickle-down economics', and that 'you can negotiate with and you can change the rules of the economy, but you cannot negotiate with the laws of science', and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: We heard from Grant Robertson, and the most interesting thing in his speech was that he said he made it to seventh form—not something I would have guessed—but I think we can be pretty sure that he didn’t do maths or economics, because he tried to argue that because Australia has a dual mandate and England doesn’t, and England had higher inflation than Australia at one point, the argument of removing the dual mandate is wrong. Now, no one that’s thought for a moment about these things would say that there’s a correlation from two data points.
acuity.explanation: Seymour restates Robertson's specific cross-country comparison and attacks its inferential basis — that a handful of data points cannot establish (or refute) a correlation. The rebuttal is aimed squarely at the argument just made and would have had to be different had Robertson argued something else, so acuity is high; the mockery of Robertson's schooling is a civility matter and the question of whether the rebuttal reasons well is a rigor matter, neither of which is scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "in the UK, which has got a central bank with a primary price stability mandate, inflation peaked at 11.1 percent. So there’s no correlation there"

acuity.statement: I’d like to speak on behalf of New Zealand First in support of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill, and on that note, I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns precede this one, so it is eligible, but the contribution engages no part of either argument. It is on the matter under debate (the bill is named) and nothing more; it would read identically whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said, which places it at the bottom of the band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Grant Robertson argued the bill is not evidence-based and that inflation outcomes show no correlation with central bank mandates, and David Seymour argued price stability is monetary policy's sole job — this statement takes up neither

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I’m proud to stand on this side of the House as part of a Government which is totally committed to reducing the cost of living and reducing inflation. The commitment to beating inflation starts with ensuring the Reserve Bank is returning to a single mandate of keeping down inflation.
acuity.explanation: Wedd follows Waititi's substantive opposition speech, which made specific claims (Māori unemployment at 7.6 percent, double the general rate; no modelling for the inflation benefit of a single mandate) and put a direct challenge about evidence. Her speech engages none of it: it asserts the single-mandate commitment and then moves to prepared constituency material on Hawke's Bay growers, on-farm inflation and the cyclone rebuild. The speech is on the matter under debate — the bill and inflation — so it is not a 0.0, but it would have read word-for-word the same whatever Waititi had said, and there is not even a gesture at the preceding argument, so it sits at the bottom of the 0.1-0.3 band. Scored only for engagement: the fact that her material is on-policy and locally concrete belongs to Focus and Specificity, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rawiri Waititi argued that repealing the employment mandate will disproportionately hit Māori and Pasifika workers and asked "Where is the modelling? Where is the evidence that this repeal will have the material effect on inflation" — this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: So it should not come as a surprise that a reasonable Government such as this National-led coalition Government has this bill as the first piece of legislation being introduced to the House in this term. It is a high priority to get the Reserve Bank’s focus back solely on getting inflation under control, but also maintaining it under control once you’re in the desired bandwidth.
acuity.explanation: Russell's immediately preceding speech made three specific arguments: the bill puts no money in pockets by Christmas, the same reordering could have been achieved under section 125 of the Reserve Bank Act without repeal, and the regulatory impact statement says Treasury would prefer the monetary policy remit. MacLeod engages none of them. He gestures at the 'first piece of legislation' theme she pressed — saying it should be no surprise this bill comes first — and then delivers prepared material on what inflation feels like, Milton Friedman and a Reagan quote. The speech would be nearly word-for-word identical had she argued something else about the bill, so this sits in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because there is a recognisable glance at the point under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "One would think that the first piece of legislation that a Government put into the House—the very first piece of legislation—would make a tangible difference right from the start."

acuity.statement: There is no evidence that these two things do not work in alignment. There is simply no evidence, and the regulatory impact statement that the Minister saw made that incredibly clear.
acuity.explanation: MacLeod's central claim was that the dual mandate failed and caused the inflation New Zealanders are paying for. Woods takes up that exact strand — denying the two objectives are in conflict and citing the regulatory impact statement against him — so you can point at what is engaged. But she contests the conclusion by flat assertion rather than engaging his reasoning (the 2019 timing argument, the Reserve Bank 'struggling ever since'), and then returns to prepared material on Labour's DNA and Grant Robertson. Partial engagement: 0.5. Note the quality of the inference is a Rigor question, not an Acuity one, and is not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David MacLeod: "Labour’s experiment of including an additional focus for the Reserve Bank has failed and we’re all paying for it—literally."

acuity.statement: I will take a moment as we’re hearing a chorus from the backbench of the Government benches that we don’t need regulatory impact statements because we had an election. Well, newsflash: elections don’t give you ultimate power. There still are requirements for you to do policy work, and our Government did all the way through.
acuity.explanation: This is unmistakably live engagement: she hears the interjection, names the proposition it carries (that an election mandate dispenses with the need for a regulatory impact statement), and rebuts it directly before returning to her argument. The passage could not have been written in advance and would not exist had Bidois stayed silent, which is the deciding test. Scored 0.9 rather than 1.0 because the thing engaged is a two-word interjection rather than a developed argument, so there is less content to take up. The combative, slightly mocking register ('newsflash') is a Civility matter and is deliberately not allowed to move this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dan Bidois: "The election!"

acuity.statement: We had a comment from the member Chlöe Swarbrick that the remit would still have reference to having regard to employment, and I want to clarify for that member that that is incorrect. We will have one operational objective in the remit, and, as has been the case in previous remits, it will be in pursuing that objective that will have regard to financial stability and other matters.
acuity.explanation: Willis takes up one specific factual claim made by another member about the content of the remit, states that it is incorrect, and then supplies the substantive correction (one operational objective, with financial stability and other matters taken into account in pursuing it). The passage could not have been written without that prior claim, and would have to change if a different claim about the remit had been made. Scored on engagement only — not on whether the correction is true (veracity) or how the surrounding speech characterises the other side (focus/civility).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "the remit would still have reference to having regard to employment" — the claim as Willis restates it from the preceding debate on the same bill.

acuity.statement: Now, the member opposite says, “They had to water it down.” The member opposite needs to remember: she’s getting rid of it. She’s getting rid of it completely. The Reserve Bank of Australia, the Federal Reserve are both completely able to manage these two things together.
acuity.explanation: Robertson takes up the specific interjected claim about Australia watering down its employment mandate and does something with it: he concedes the premise implicitly and turns it into a contrast with the Minister's own bill, which removes the employment objective entirely, then cites both the RBA and the Fed as counter-examples. The passage would not exist if Willis had not interjected that line, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 because he does not dispute or examine the substance of the "watering down" claim itself, he pivots from it to the comparative point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "They had to water it down, you know that."

acuity.statement: Once again, we have there in black and white—as myself and the Minister, when she was previously a member of the Finance and Expenditure Committee, heard elucidated time and time again from the Reserve Bank Governor—that, ultimately, there was not all too much difference that was coming out of the monetary policy committee as a result of the dual mandate.
acuity.explanation: The speech is squarely on the matter under debate and is aimed at the Minister's earlier remarks rather than at the member who immediately preceded her, so it engages no part of Robertson's argument. Prepared material on the right subject with a gesture at the debate puts it at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band; the speech would read essentially identically had Robertson made a different argument about the dual mandate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Grant Robertson argued that the Reserve Bank's governors said the dual mandate "did not alter one iota their focus on inflation" and that the bill is "a solution in search of a problem", and this statement does not take up his argument — it arrives at an adjacent conclusion from the member's own material (the tabled remit review and her own select committee recollection) rather than engaging his.

acuity.statement: I think we’ve heard some fine contributions on the theory of inflation and Milton Friedman and the like. But essentially what we’re dealing with here is a real-world issue that, as Mr Stephenson just pointed out, families are hurting, cost of living is hurting, our business community and our farmers are hurting with record-high interest rates that’s driven as a result of the record-high inflation.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding turn — Stephenson's cost-of-living point — and explicitly sets aside his Friedman/theory material as 'fluff', extending the hardship claim to farmers and business. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Todd Stephenson: "that’s affecting households with increases in mortgages and petrol prices and grocery prices" (and his Milton Friedman quotation)

acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the removal of the dual mandate — and gestures at the interest-rate consequences the previous speaker raised, but engages no part of Patterson's or Stephenson's actual argument. The surrounding speech (job losses, rushed pre-Christmas legislation) would read identically whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Patterson spoke about record-high interest rates hurting families, farmers and business and about being persuaded by the Minister of Finance, and this statement does not take up either claim; it is prepared opposition to the bill's mechanism.

acuity.explanation: Directly takes the causal claim made two turns earlier — that the previous Government's spending and the dual mandate produced New Zealand's inflation — and tests it against cross-country CPI data, which she tables in the House. The speech would have to change if the preceding ACT contribution had attributed inflation to something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Todd Stephenson: "this large increase in Government spending has had consequences" / "The last Government’s output certainly didn’t match the amount it was spending."

It engages his premise squarely, though it answers the broader 1980s reform programme rather than the inflation-target claim itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Todd Stephenson: "there’s actually nothing wrong with going back to 1989, when this was put in place and it worked"

acuity.statement: I just want to talk about what happens when you try and do two things and don't do either well. The interesting thing I will speak on is public transport. acuity.responding_to: "So these things are not in competition." — Helen White, who argued at length that maximum sustainable employment sits alongside price stability rather than competing with it

acuity.responding_to: Catherine Wedd: "It’s time we focus on hard-working New Zealanders and reducing the cost of living."

It’s exactly the opposite of what they’ve been talking about.

acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "he was certainly a supporter of what we were doing, and what we were doing was creating jobs" (and his unemployment figures for 2018)

They’re saying that the National Party or the coalition doesn’t care about employment, doesn’t care about people, etc. It’s complete and utter nonsense. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Government doesn’t care about employment. That’s what this bill is telling us." — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: So I’d just like to back up those sentiments from the former Minister because, as we’ve well canvassed—and, actually, as is reflected in the monetary policy remit review from June 2023—it’s pretty clear in black and white from the Reserve Bank of New Zealand that there hadn’t been any meaningful impact or other decisions that would have been made had they not had that dual mandate and solely the focus on price stability.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Robertson's precise question — whether the dual mandate diluted the Reserve Bank's inflation focus — and does something with it, supplying the June 2023 monetary policy remit review as evidence for the negative before pressing the Minister for counter-evidence. The speech would have to change had Robertson asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "what advice, if any, has she received that there was less of a focus on inflation because of the dual mandate in the time that it has been in place?"

acuity.statement: As I’ve alluded to before, we haven’t had a select committee stage in this bill, but I have heard from a number of people, so I do want to bring some of those letters to the House so that they at least inform the discussions as we go through this part of the bill.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the preceding turns — the absence of select committee scrutiny — and acts on it by substituting constituent correspondence for submissions. It engages nothing of the specific question about advice on the dual mandate, and the bulk of the turn is a letter read into the record, so this is partial engagement rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "hasn’t gone off to a select committee, hasn’t had the ability to be scrutinised"

I would note that without amending the Act, the monetary policy committee (MPC) would still be required to have regard to maximum sustainable employment.
acuity.explanation: Identifies Swarbrick's specific alternative — amending the remit alone rather than the Act — and gives the reason it was rejected, that the statutory duty to have regard to maximum sustainable employment would survive a remit change. Directly engages the content of the question put, not merely its topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "I wanted to ask the Minister if she meaningfully explored any of those other options, particularly on the monetary policy committee (MPC) remit only, or the Order in Council"

acuity.explanation: Engages the Minister's stated justification head-on, noting that she answered on the value of signalling clarity while leaving unanswered whether any advice showed the dual mandate actually compromised the Bank's inflation focus, and sets the Governor's repeated statements against it. The intervention is shaped entirely by what Willis had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "we have received advice that there is value in amending the Act to signal a greater focus on price stability than that which could be achieved through a new remit alone"

acuity.statement: Because I totally appreciate—as she herself alluded to—that the remit review in June 2023 spoke to the need for prioritisation of explicitly that dual mandate and particularly the foreshadowing or the primacy of the price stability focus. But again, my point was that that could be achieved through a change to the remit, as again was recommended by her officials.
acuity.explanation: Swarbrick follows Woods' line of questioning about what advice the Minister sought on alternatives to repeal, and takes up the same strand — that the policy aim could be achieved by another mechanism (a remit change rather than a statutory secondary objective). But she is mainly pursuing her own previously-put questions rather than engaging Woods' specific point about international best practice and the dual mandate comparators, so this is partial engagement with the topic and the adjacent strand, not with the claim just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "did she ask for any advice around having employment as a secondary objective within the legislation"

acuity.statement: In answer to the member’s question: yes, I did receive advice that the dual mandate could affect monetary policy decisions, and in particular—as I have stressed—this is not just about the decisions the Reserve Bank makes but also the interpretation of those decisions. The Reserve Bank itself has supported the intention of clarifying its focus on inflation.
acuity.explanation: Willis takes up one of the three questions just put to her — the evidence/advice on whether the dual mandate affected Reserve Bank decision making — and supplies a direct answer to it, adding the interpretation point and the Bank's own position. The speech would be different had the preceding turn not pressed on advice. But she leaves untouched the two strands Swarbrick flagged as outstanding (what the remit will contain, and whether employment or house prices feature in it), so engagement is partial rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "the evidence that she has on whether there has been any meaningful impact on decision making by the RBNZ"

acuity.statement: When the Minister spoke before, she used the words “could” and “would be possible that it might happen”. That’s not, Mr Chair, with respect, what I asked. What I asked was whether or not the Minister had been advised that there had been some kind of impact, and the answer is no.
acuity.explanation: This takes the Minister's immediately preceding words and does something specific with them: it isolates her modal verbs ("could", "possible"), distinguishes an advised possibility from an advised actual effect, and draws the consequence that no evidence of actual impact was received. The speech is wholly contingent on what Willis just said — a different answer would have required a different reply. Scored on engagement only; the soundness of the inference and the truth of the characterisation are other attributes' business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "yes, I did receive advice that the dual mandate could affect monetary policy decisions"

acuity.statement: I just want to move, second, to the question of the content of the remit and the charter. I want to assure the member Chlöe Swarbrick that we will retain the flexible inflation targeting regime under which the response of the Reserve Bank to inflation is tempered by considering the impact on other factors in the real economy. I will publish an updated remit and charter upon passage of this Act.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Swarbrick's first question directly — what survives in the remit as opposed to the statute — and commits to publishing the updated remit, so the passage would read differently had she not asked it. But it answers the remit question only in general terms (flexible inflation targeting retained) without saying where employment or house price sustainability sit, and leaves her second and third questions (evidence of deprioritised price stability; who the market participants are) untouched. Partial, pointable engagement, then back to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "but the question still remains as to whether she thinks it should be within the broader monetary policy committee’s remit" — Chlöe Swarbrick

acuity.statement: But have they? That’s the question you’re not answering. Why don’t you answer the question—have they?
acuity.explanation: Pins the exact gap in the sentence just spoken: Willis moved from 'have they been in conflict' to the modal 'could move in opposite directions', and this interjection isolates that slip and demands the factual answer. It could not have been delivered against any other wording, which is the test. Short, and pointed at the content rather than the person.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "often the objectives of price stability and maximum sustainable employment will align. However, the objectives could move in opposite directions" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: So reducing the possibility of volatility—Mrs Woods—in future rates of inflation is actually a priority for this Government.
acuity.explanation: Woods asked whether the two objectives have in fact been in conflict. This acknowledges her by name and answers a different question — the Government's priorities — restating the general position rather than supplying the historical instance asked for. On the topic under debate, but engages no part of the challenge, which puts it in the low band rather than at a partial 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "But have they? That’s the question you’re not answering." — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: Finally, I want to note that there are a number of amendments that have been tabled and suggested by the member Hon Grant Robertson, who can’t seem to make up his mind what the purpose of the Reserve Bank Act has been, because I can count several different ideas he has, which is rather symptomatic of the member—that he couldn’t just land on one thing.
acuity.explanation: Names the amendments and their mover but engages the content of none of them — no clause, no mechanism, no reason any one of them fails. The count of 'several different ideas' is turned into a character observation and then a pivot to the Government's own line, which is the mere-reference pattern rather than engagement. Scored low for unresponsiveness only; whether the remark is fair or well-reasoned belongs to other attributes, which I have not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I still have a few points that I’d like the Minister to address" — the amendments referred to were tabled by Grant Robertson, whose only preceding turn in this window is a point of order; nothing in the preceding debate content is taken up.

acuity.statement: But this links back to why I’m standing in the Chamber and wanting to ask the Minister a question; it’s around perceptions. And so there is a perception, sometimes—by this Government, who has only just started—that there are a couple of failings in the rest of society. acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford, as she states the question: "what evidence base we have for this bill given that we don’t have a regulatory impact statement".

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Brooke van Velden had just argued that the 2021 regulatory impact statement still applies and that individual and collective agreements are more flexible than fair pay agreements, and this statement does not take either up.

The Parliamentary Counsel Office have advised that it’s not standard practice in drafting a repeal bill to include a purpose clause, because the purpose of a repeal bill is to repeal a bill.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Belich's specific question — why the bill has no purpose clause — restates it accurately and supplies a substantive answer (PCO drafting advice that repeal bills do not carry purpose clauses). acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "The first is: why isn’t there a purpose clause in this document and why isn’t there more detail about what it seeks to achieve?"

acuity.explanation: Engages the precise point just put — the replacement of section 132(2) and the loss of the overtime and penalty rate wording — and rebuts its premise by explaining the change is deliberate rather than a drafting error, since the wording was itself inserted by the Fair Pay Agreements Act. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "I think that the amendment that I’ve tabled corrects a mistake in the drafting of this bill."

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "by the ACT Party’s own principles of legislative quality, an analysis should be done of the costs and benefits of this legislation"

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "What I want to know is what analysis has been done of the costs and the benefits of having fair pay agreements on the one hand"

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "Because there have not been any fair pay agreements in effect, it would be impossible to review what a system that had never been in place would look like after three years"

acuity.explanation: The question goes straight at the premise van Velden had just asserted — that industry-wide minimum standards harm businesses and therefore workers and families — and demands the evidence base for it, from the standpoint of a small-business owner. That is engaging the specific claim, not just the topic, and the question would have to be different had the Minister argued on other grounds. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "I consider that the fair pay agreements system is a blunt tool that affects all employees and all employers within scope within a particular industry, and that would negatively impact on businesses"

acuity.statement: Now, if we talk about increasing productivity, this has been the rationale of those on the right for as long as anyone in this House can remember—for as long as anyone in this House can remember: if only we can increase productivity, then workers would be better off. The problem with that, of course, is that productivity is linked to wages, and there is a reason why Australia and other countries that follow what was in place in the Fair Pay Agreements Act—the Act that this bill, in Part 2, seeks to repeal—have higher productivity: the two go hand in hand. Since 1991, New Zealand’s productivity has not kept up with other countries that have maintained what is in the Fair Pay Agreements Act.
acuity.explanation: The preceding turn in this window is Carmel Sepuloni's demand to know the productivity losses flowing from repealing fair pay agreements. McAnulty takes up that same productivity strand and develops it — arguing productivity and wages are causally linked and citing comparator countries — but he directs his engagement at the Minister's earlier answer to Adrian Rurawhe rather than at Sepuloni's specific cover-sheet question, and then moves into his own prepared material on deregulation and the Act's purpose clause. Partial engagement: one strand of the preceding contribution is clearly picked up and argued with, the specific demand put is not answered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carmel Sepuloni: "I want to know what the productivity loss will be for those workforces because of the fact that we do not have fair pay agreements in place"

How will the Minister mitigate the disproportionate impact of stagnant lower wages for women without FPA?
acuity.explanation: This follows a substantive turn by Kieran McAnulty arguing that productivity and wages go hand in hand and that the Government has offered no tangible alternative to fair pay agreements. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Kieran McAnulty argued that productivity is linked to wages and that the Minister has offered only "a theory and a loose promise" in place of fair pay agreements, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.responding_to: Darleen Tana, whose question the Minister reproduces in taking it up: "you asked what evidence I have that small businesses don’t actually want to sign up for this type of agreement" (the question was put in an earlier turn of the same committee debate, which is identified in this turn rather than reproduced in this window)

acuity.statement: But we don’t consider, as a Government, that we wish to have any exemptions to the repeal, because we believe that there is a better way to improve the conditions of workers, for business and employees, without having fair pay agreements, and that is through increased productivity; that is through reducing regulation.

acuity.statement: It was very difficult to listen to the contribution from the Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety, because I have to say it was rather patronising.
acuity.explanation: A reference to the preceding speaker that engages none of her content. The productivity-and-deregulation argument was squarely available to rebut and is left untouched; this sentence would read identically whatever the Minister had argued, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band, with 0.2 rather than 0.1 because it at least gestures at the contribution just made in the same debate. Scored on responsiveness alone — the dismissive framing is a civility question and is not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Brooke van Velden argued immediately before that no exemptions to the repeal are warranted because conditions are better lifted through increased productivity and reduced regulation, and this statement does not take up any part of that — it characterises the manner of her contribution and then turns to the amendments on the Table.

acuity.statement: Coming back to the member: because she’s asked for it to be specifically about statistical data in relation to those specific areas that we’d already touched on that does not actually exist, that question is not possible to answer.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What's the productivity loss to not having fair pay agreements, is my other part of it." — Carmel Sepuloni (interjection)

acuity.statement: I live in Ōtepoti—Dunedin—and for years bus companies have been engaged in a race to the bottom in terms of wages, with drivers working split shifts and often engaging in second jobs just to put food on the table. Dunedin bus drivers have even had to pee behind bushes and limit their water intake—not like in the Chamber—so that they can keep at work because there are no toilets. So the Minister might argue that repealing fair pay is just tidying things up, but I'd argue that it's far tidier and healthier to provide good conditions and support bus drivers in Aotearoa rather than encouraging them to head to Australia.
acuity.explanation: Willis follows two substantive Opposition turns and takes up one strand of them: Jackson's claim that bus drivers are quitting because conditions are intolerable, and Andersen's "race to the bottom" framing, which he extends with Dunedin evidence of split shifts and no toilets. He does not engage Jackson's actual question (what consultation the Minister has had) or Andersen's specific clause 8 review proposal, and the second half moves to his own prepared question about Australian pay rates. Partial, pointable engagement rather than a rebuttal or direct answer, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It's normal for four or five bus drivers to quit each week because the conditions are just too much for them." — Willie Jackson (Ginny Andersen immediately before also warned of a "race to the bottom")

So the new clause 6 that is proposed to amend this bill is that the Royal assent of the bill is contingent on a review by the International Labour Organization (ILO), ensuring that New Zealand is compliant with all international obligations including ILO conventions and free-trade agreements.
acuity.explanation: Andersen follows the Minister's reply to her own amendment but engages none of its content: she neither contests the claim that the Minister will commission her own market advice nor the Minister's reason for refusing the amendment. She resumes her prepared sequence of amendments. It is squarely on the bill under debate, and there is a gesture at continuity ("pick up where I was likely to continue previously"), so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Brooke van Velden had just answered her directly — "I expect to do my own advice and information on the market, independent from the member, and that does not need to be in this bill" — and this statement does not take that refusal up, moving straight to a further amendment.

acuity.statement: I usually allow a range of members to speak before I respond, but I must respond to that statement. Nobody will be worse off this Christmas because there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised. Nobody will be having lower wages because of the repeal of this Act.
acuity.explanation: She breaks her own stated practice of waiting in order to take up the specific claim Andersen had just made, and rebuts it on its own terms with the reason it fails — no fair pay agreement has been concluded, so no worker's pay is reduced by the repeal. The reply would be impossible had the preceding speech said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "that will be earning less this Christmas, that will afford less on their table, fewer Christmas presents"

acuity.statement: The other thing that I do want to ask the Minister again is what is the plan if it doesn’t work? Can we surely put aside the differences that we have fundamentally or philosophically tonight and look at why the Minister wouldn’t support our amendment to ensure that there is a review, that we continue to be proud to grow, as I said, good employers to be great employers; good employees, employees to be able to be looked after; and the most vulnerable are not targeted, because at times that’s how it’s coming across.
acuity.explanation: She takes up one strand of the Minister's position — the commitment-based refusal to vary the repeal — and argues it should not block a review amendment, which does not continue the system for any sector. That is a real engagement with the Minister's stated reason. But she does not touch the claim in the turn immediately before hers (that nobody will be worse off this Christmas), and much of the surrounding material is prepared argument for her own new clause 8, so it is partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "Allowing the system to continue for one sector would go against the commitment that we brought to this House, but also our commitment to New Zealand voters"

acuity.statement: This is a clawback bill. This bill, to repeal the ground-breaking fair pay agreement legislation in New Zealand, is a clawback for workers, and I disagree wholeheartedly with the Minister’s statement earlier that workers will not be worse off.
acuity.explanation: Boyack follows a substantive turn by van Velden, who argued that a three-year review clause cannot work because no fair pay agreements were ever finalised, that employees need not join a union to be covered, and that repeal avoids engaging international obligations. Boyack takes up none of those three points. She gestures at the debate by contesting a ministerial claim that workers will not be worse off, but that claim was made 'earlier' and not in the turn she follows, and her speech is her prepared case for two amendments she had already tabled. If van Velden had made a different argument on the same clauses, this speech would read identically — hence the low band, with 0.3 rather than 0.1 for the gesture at the Minister's position.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Brooke van Velden argued 'there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised' and so a review of the repeal's sector impacts 'does not work in practice', and this statement does not take that up — it disputes a ministerial statement made earlier, outside the turn it follows.

acuity.statement: Speaking to the member’s question, no. The policy intent is quite correctly captured by the title of the bill. It’s pretty plain and simple and we have a coalition commitment to repeal the fair pay agreements by Christmas, which is what we intend to do.
acuity.explanation: Boyack put two direct questions to the Minister — will she support the retitling amendment, and will she support the three-year commencement amendment. Van Velden answers the title question squarely ('no') and gives her reason: the existing title captures the policy intent, and the coalition commitment is to repeal by Christmas, which also disposes of the three-year delay. The reply is unmistakably shaped by what was just said and would not exist without it. Short of 1.0 because she engages the amendments' framing rather than Boyack's substantive argument that three years of operation would supply the evidence the Government says it wants.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'will she support a proper title for this bill that properly reflects what the Government is doing here, which is a clawback' — Rachel Boyack

My amendment really goes to the heart, I think, of the Government’s justification for this bill, which is, essentially, that we’ve had an election and the Government wants to implement their commitments from during the election.
acuity.explanation: Van Velden had just rested her refusal on an electoral mandate — a coalition commitment to repeal by Christmas. Belich names that exact justification as the thing her amendment is aimed at, and then offers a referendum threshold as the way to test whether the mandate is real. The speech is built on the reason the Minister had just given moments before, so substituting a different justification would force it to change. Not 1.0 because she characterises the mandate argument and pivots to her own amendment rather than rebutting its reasoning in detail.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'we have a coalition commitment to repeal the fair pay agreements by Christmas, which is what we intend to do' — Brooke van Velden

But, in relationship to the commencement, reflecting on some of the previous contributions from the Minister, I hear that she has been saying that this is part of the coalition agreement and that the intent is to pass it before Christmas.

acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "I also wanted to support my colleague Rachel Boyack’s amendment to the change of the title, which I believe is more correct in the nature of the bill."

I think the point needs expanding a little bit because what we have in this situation is very, very little evidence, a lot of hunch about what will happen next.

acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "Throughout the debate there also has been a lack of ability to produce evidence as to why this must be repealed"

So we are reversing all other changes but retaining this one, so it’s not in the bill.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the specific answer the preceding turn asked for — explaining that the GST-exclusive provision is retained precisely because the bill is silent on it, which is why Belich could not find it. acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "I wonder if the Minister could point me to exactly where those retained amendments are."

On the matter under debate, with a glance at it rather than engagement.

acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "Yeah, 'I know what's best for us.'"

acuity.statement: Today is a day where a whole lot of New Zealanders lose a brighter future. What had been established over many, many years was that we had a problem. We had a problem of a low-wage economy where a whole lot of people were sinking, and we have the consequences of that, which we see every day.
acuity.explanation: White follows Jackson in the same debate and her opening is squarely on the matter under debate — the repeal and the low-wage economy — so it is not a 0.0. But it engages no part of what Jackson had just argued; the references she does answer ('the comment that we'd had earlier about bus drivers', 'when you talk about good employers') are to claims made earlier in the debate and not present in the preceding turn, so there is nothing in the immediately preceding contribution I can point at as engaged. This is prepared material on the right subject with a gesture at the debate, which the rubric puts at 0.3 and caps there because the engagement cannot be pointed at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willie Jackson spoke about Helen Kelly's work on fair pay bargaining, Jim Bolger's change of heart, and a Treasury warning that repeal would hurt Māori, Pasifika and women workers, and this statement takes up none of it.

acuity.statement: So I encourage those members—yeah, picture these workers. Because clearly the Minister chose to not engage with any of those workers when it came to the substance of this bill.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Bates' claim that Government members are engaged with workers and turns it into a specific counter-charge that the Minister did not engage workers on the substance of the bill. It engages one strand of the interjection — the claim to be listening — rather than the food-bank evidence itself, and then returns to prepared material about submissions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I was at a food bank on Friday, food bank on Monday. Serving food on Monday. Don't tell me we're not looking at workers." — Carl Bates

acuity.statement: Today is a great day. It is the day of the liberation of New Zealand from the Fair Pay Agreements Act (FPA). The FPA is simply a mandated union bargaining tool and we will not stand for it.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate but indifferent to what preceded it. Substituting a different critique of the repeal in the prior turn would require no change to a word of this; there is no gesture at the consultation or coverage arguments just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March argued the Government took no submissions and gave no reason for it, and that 200,000 to 300,000 workers would have benefited from fair pay agreements, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: New Zealand First supports the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill for the reason that the Fair Pay Agreements Act is bad legislation—it’s the reason why we put the handbrake on it when we were last in Government and didn’t let it see the light of day. Despite the protestations of the members opposite, these are highly complex agreements that severely disadvantage regional employers.
acuity.explanation: Engages the opposition case in part: it answers the claim that the agreements would improve conditions by asserting they are too complex and disadvantage regional employers. But "the protestations of the members opposite" is a generic reference rather than engagement with a specific claim, and the speech then proceeds to prepared material and to a speech (Camilla Belich's) from outside this exchange.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "fair pay agreements were one of the things in place to guarantee improvements to the working conditions of those workers" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: Well, that’s the union’s problem; it’s not the Government’s problem to deal that out.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question actually put, and on its own terms: it concedes the gap and locates responsibility for it outside government rather than deflecting or changing the subject. Whether the answer is adequate is a separate question from whether it engages — on engagement it is squarely aimed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "80 percent are not unionised. What about them?" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: To be really clear, the repeal of this legislation is an absolute assault on workers. There are all sorts of guises and pretences based on belief—is what we keep hearing from the Minister: based on belief. It’s not; it is a direct assault on workers.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the subject under debate, addressed to workers and unions rather than to the argument just made. The glancing reference to what "we keep hearing from the Minister" is aimed at a framing from earlier in the bill's passage, not at Patterson's market-forces case, so the speech would be unchanged had he argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mark Patterson argued the agreements were superfluous because low unemployment, employer demand and existing collective bargaining mean market forces already protect good workers, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: This year, I door-knocked and called over 9,000 people personally across the Whanganui electorate. It may surprise members opposite that this included thousands of workers and New Zealanders of every background.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the charge that Government members do not carry workers' voices and answers it with his own canvassing, with "New Zealanders of every background" picking up Davidson's groups. It answers the topic — who speaks for workers — rather than her specific claim about systemic inequities in low-paid sectors, and the rest is prepared.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We are bringing your voices into the halls of power" — Marama Davidson, whose speech claimed the repeal hits sectors overrepresented by Māori, Pasifika, women, young people and disabled people

acuity.statement: They’re all wrong, apparently—even business leaders, according to Simon Court. He just said they’re all wrong. So business leaders, economic leaders, Simon Court from ACT thinks you’re wrong.
acuity.explanation: She picks up Court's interjection and names it, but does nothing with its content: she restates it back and turns it into a label for ACT rather than defending the claim that commentators, business leaders and unions agree with her. The rest of the passage is prepared material on Australian enterprise bargaining that would have been delivered unchanged. A mere reference plus a pivot sits in the low band, not at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "They're all wrong." — Simon Court

acuity.statement: Despite the rhetoric from the other side of the House over there, our business owners in the Wairarapa electorate take their responsibilities to their employees seriously, in good times and bad. If they’re forced to lay off staff, reduce production, or close their doors, everyone suffers, and the fair pay agreement will do nothing—nothing—to lift the productivity that New Zealand desperately needs.
acuity.explanation: He takes up one strand of Boyack's preceding speech — her accounts of employers mistreating workers — with a direct counter-assertion that employers in his electorate treat staff responsibly, so the engagement is pointable. But it is a bare assertion rather than a reply to her actual case about sector-wide minimum standards (public holidays on a Tuesday-to-Saturday roster, bus drivers' split shifts), and the productivity line is prepared material that would stand whatever she had said. Partial engagement, hence mid-low rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I just find it so offensive that people on the other side of this House actually think that stories about workers being mistreated in the workplace" — Rachel Boyack

acuity.statement: We heard from the Minister that he’s had an opportunity to focus on this regressive and fiscally irresponsible piece of legislation, as it currently stands. He’s talked about fiscal irresponsibility. He has talked about how we would be taking the money from hard workers and, effectively, giving it to the rich. How fiscally responsible is it, then, for the Tesla-loving Prime Minister’s household to be able to access the very rebate that his Government seeks to remove?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific equity argument Brown had just built the case on (the 'reverse Robin Hood' claim that the scheme taxed workers to subsidise the wealthy) and turns it against him with the Prime Minister's own rebate. The speech would be different had Brown argued on different grounds — it is pegged to Brown's own framing and quotes his terms back in order to invert them. Short of 1.0 because it does not dispute the reasoning or the figures Brown gave; it answers the premise with a hypocrisy charge rather than engaging whether the distributional claim holds.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this policy was taking from those who didn’t have a choice and giving it to people who could afford to pay for those vehicles" — Simeon Brown
